Zipporah
zih-POR-uh
n. (proper)
Hebrew Tsipporah, a little bird or sparrow, from tsippor, a bird. One of the seven daughters of Jethro priest of Midian, she became Moses’ wife at the well, and it was her hand that performed the circumcision that saved his life on the way back to Egypt.

Biblical Definition

Zipporah is the Midianite wife of Moses, given him by Jethro after he drove off the shepherds at the well: Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter (Exodus 2:21). She bore him Gershom and Eliezer. The passage that fixes her place in Scripture is the strangest in the book. On the road back to Egypt, at the inn, the LORD met him, and sought to kill him — Moses, going to demand that Pharaoh release God’s covenant son, had not put the covenant sign on his own. Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me (Exodus 4:25), and the LORD let him go. She acted, and her words show she did not like it; obedience is recorded, not enthusiasm. Afterward Moses sent her back to her father, and Jethro brought her and the two sons to the camp at Sinai (Exodus 18:2). The one other reference to Moses’ wife is Numbers 12, where Miriam and Aaron spoke against him because of the Ethiopian woman he had married — and God struck Miriam leprous, defending His servant’s marriage without qualification.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no ZIPPORAH entry. The Hebrew means a bird, the feminine of tsippor, the ordinary word for a small bird throughout the Old Testament.

ZIPPORAH, n. — The daughter of Jethro (Reuel) priest of Midian, and the wife of Moses (Exodus 2:21).

The name is Hebrew for a bird or sparrow; the masculine tsippor appears in Leviticus 14 of the birds used in the cleansing of the leper.

Her sons were Gershom, a stranger here (Exodus 2:22), and Eliezer, the God of my father was mine help (Exodus 18:4).

Exodus 4:24-26 is one of the most difficult passages in the Pentateuch, and Zipporah is its acting figure.

Whether the Ethiopian woman of Numbers 12:1 is Zipporah under another description or a second wife has been debated since the fathers; the text does not settle it.

Key Scripture

Exodus 2:21 — "And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter."

Exodus 4:25 — "Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me."

Exodus 18:2 — "Then Jethro, Moses’ father in law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her back,"

Numbers 12:1 — "And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman."

Genesis 17:14 — "And the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken my covenant."

Modern Corruption

Exodus 4:24-26 is skipped in almost every retelling of Moses’ life, and the omission removes the sharpest lesson in the Pentateuch about a leader’s household — that God will not send a man to demand covenant obedience of others while he neglects the covenant sign in his own house.

expand to see more

God had just told Moses to say to Pharaoh, Israel is my son, even my firstborn… let my son go, that he may serve me. On the road, at the inn, the LORD sought to kill him, and the remedy Zipporah applied identifies the offence exactly: a son of Abraham in Moses’ own tent was uncircumcised, in plain breach of Genesis 17:14. The mediator of the covenant was going to prosecute a covenant claim against Egypt with the covenant broken in his own household. The application to the ministry is direct and is made explicit in 1 Timothy 3: a man who does not rule his own house well cannot take care of the church of God. The passage is skipped because it is severe, and it is severe because the office is.

Zipporah herself deserves better than she usually gets. She is often read as resentful, and her words — a bloody husband art thou to me — are certainly not pious. But she is the one who understood what was required, took the flint, and did it, at an hour when her husband was apparently unable. Scripture repeatedly records obedience rendered without warm feeling and does not despise it; the son who said I will not and afterward repented and went is the one who did his father’s will. A Christian wife holding a household to the covenant when her husband has let it slip is doing what Zipporah did at the inn, and it saved Moses’ life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tsipporah (H6855), a bird, feminine of tsippor (H6833); her father is Yithro (H3503), Jethro, also called Reuel.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tsipporah (H6855) — Zipporah; a little bird, a sparrow.

Hebrew tsippor (H6833) — a bird; the common noun, used of the sparrow alone upon the housetop (Psalm 102:7).

Hebrew tsor (H6864) — a flint, a sharp stone; the instrument she used (Exodus 4:25).

Hebrew chathan damim — a bridegroom of blood; the phrase the Authorized Version renders a bloody husband.

Hebrew Gereshom (H1647) — Gershom; for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land (Exodus 2:22).

Usage

"He gave Moses Zipporah his daughter (Exodus 2:21) — the marriage made in Midian exile."

"Then Zipporah took a sharp stone (Exodus 4:25) — the wife who did what the mediator had not."

"Because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married (Numbers 12:1) — the marriage God defended against Miriam."
